```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

gPIPE implements the PIPE design (product of independent beta probabilities
escalation) for drug-combination dose-finding trials. It covers two designs:

- the original PIPE design of Mander & Sweeting (2015) for the maximum
  tolerated dose (MTD) contour, with binary toxicity outcomes;
- PIPE with epsilon-tapering of Cheung et al. (2022), for the minimum
  effective dose (MED) or the MTD.

```{r}
library(gPIPE)
```

## The idea in one paragraph

Each dose combination k has a parameter (toxicity probability, or mean
efficacy) and a target threshold theta. PIPE estimates which combinations lie
above theta, as a 0/1 vector gamma, assuming that the parameter grows with the
dose of every drug. So the "above" set is closed upwards. Among all such sets
it picks the one that best fits the posterior probabilities
p_k = P(parameter_k > theta | data). The asymmetry `eps` makes it harder to
declare the favourable side (safe for MTD, effective for MED); `eps = 0.5` is
the original, symmetric PIPE. With epsilon-tapering, `eps` moves from 0.5 to
its final value over the trial, which explores more early on.

## Dose grid

A `DoseGrid` lists the combinations and their partial order. Combinations are
numbered in array order: the first drug's level changes fastest.

```{r}
grid <- DoseGrid(levels = c(A = 4, B = 4))
n_combos(grid)
head(combo_labels(grid))
```

## Mander & Sweeting design (MTD)

`ms_design()` sets priors from their medians and a prior strength (a + b). A
total strength of 1 over the grid is the "weak" prior of the paper.

```{r}
prior_median <- c(outer(c(0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16), c(0, 0.06, 0.12, 0.18), `+`))
ms <- ms_design(grid, theta = 0.2, prior_median = prior_median,
                prior_strength = 1 / 16, N = 50, cohort = 1)
```

Trial data are a data frame with one row per patient, in the order treated:
the dose level of each drug, and the outcome `y` (1 = toxicity).

```{r}
data <- data.frame(A = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 2), B = c(1, 2, 2, 2, 3), y = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0))
estimate(ms, data)
```

`next_dose()` gives the doses the design may give next, with their
probabilities. Here they are the doses closest to the estimated contour within
one level of the current dose, among those that pass the safety rule.

```{r}
nd <- next_dose(ms, data)
nd$candidates
```

## Simulating operating characteristics

`simulate()` runs whole trials under a true scenario. The result holds one
row per trial and, over trials x combinations, the patients treated and the
final dose set (for M&S, the recommended phase II doses).

```{r}
truth <- matrix(c(0.04, 0.08, 0.12, 0.16, 0.10, 0.14, 0.18, 0.22,
                  0.16, 0.20, 0.24, 0.28, 0.22, 0.26, 0.30, 0.34), 4, 4)
sim <- simulate(ms, nsim = 20, seed = 1, truth = truth)
sim
```

Use many more trials (for example 2000) for real operating characteristics.

## Cheung's epsilon-tapering design (MED)

`cheung_design()` defaults to an MED target with normal outcomes. While there
is too little data to estimate the outcome variance, `sigma0` is used. The
first patient gets the top dose, and later doses are drawn from Cheung's
sampling set S1 u S0 near the estimated boundary.

```{r}
grid5 <- DoseGrid(levels = c(A = 5, B = 5))
med <- cheung_design(grid5, theta = 0.5, eps = 0.05, N = 60, sigma0 = 1)
truth <- list(mean = outer(seq(0, 0.6, length.out = 5), seq(0, 0.6, length.out = 5), `+`),
              sd = 1)
sim_med <- simulate(med, nsim = 10, seed = 2, truth = truth)
sim_med
```

The final MED set is the minimal effective combinations of the final estimate,
which uses `eps` itself.

## Summaries and plots

`summary()` turns a simulation into the tables papers report. Each metric
follows the definition of its source paper: FDR and TPR (Cheung et al.),
the proportion of trials that pick a true MTD (Riviere et al.), and the
recommendation table by true-parameter band (Mander & Sweeting). Combinations
within `band` of `theta` count as indifferent; the default band for MTD is
0.25 theta.

```{r}
summary(sim)
```

`plot()` shows the percentage of trials selecting each combination, or the
mean number of patients treated. It needs ggplot2.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 4, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(sim)
```

## Calibrating epsilon

`calibrate_eps()` finds the largest `eps` whose false discovery rate stays
within `alpha`, over an ensemble of monotone true scenarios. It searches by
bisection and reuses the same random numbers at every `eps`. The example is
kept small; use many more trials and scenarios in practice.

```{r}
g3 <- DoseGrid(levels = c(A = 3, B = 3))
des <- cheung_design(g3, theta = 0.3, eps = 0.5, target = "MTD", outcome = "binary",
                     prior_a = 0.3, prior_b = 0.7, N = 20)
cal <- calibrate_eps(des, n_scenarios = 3, nsim = 10, tol = 0.1, seed = 1)
cal
```

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 5, fig.height = 3.5}
plot(cal)
```

The calibrated design is `cal@design`.

## References

- Mander, A. P. and Sweeting, M. J. (2015). A product of independent beta
  probabilities dose escalation design for dual-agent phase I trials.
  *Statistics in Medicine*, 34, 1261--1276. doi:10.1002/sim.6434.
- Cheung, Y. K., Chandereng, T. and Diaz, K. M. (2022). A novel framework to
  estimate multidimensional minimum effective doses using asymmetric
  posterior gain and epsilon-tapering. *Annals of Applied Statistics*,
  16(3), 1445--1458. doi:10.1214/21-AOAS1549.
